items.title: A $20M fine stalks Los Angeles over delay of a new housing project
items.description: Blocking a Los Angeles housing development over a mountain lion could cost the city $20 million or more and still fail to stop the project. L.A. has 60 days to approve 398 homes at Woodland Hills Country Club or face a lawsuit that could cost it that much, according to a letter from the club's attorney, Dave Rand, sent to the city Friday. A judge could order the city to pay punitive damages for the delay and rule that the development still must proceed, Rand confirmed with HousingWire TBD . If the club prevails in its case for damages provided under the Housing Accountability Act, the city would owe fines of at least $19.9 million. It would also owe attorney's fees, costs and compensatory damages. The letter says that exposure "could therefore cost the city well in excess of $20 million." Rand wrote that he can't imagine the risk to taxpayers "is worth it." Rand wrote that the city's denial violated both Assembly Bill 2011 and the Housing Accountability Act. The letter invokes AB 712, which extends any limitation period by 60 days from the letter's date. That keeps the club's legal options open while the city weighs its response. The damages math on housing development Rand explained the fine math on social media. The base fine is $10,000 per unit for a violation, and $50,000 per unit for a finding of bad faith. AB 712 raises the fine to an automatic $50,000 per unit if the city has lost in court at least once in the same housing element cycle. At $50,000 a unit, 398 homes come to the $19.9 million cited in the letter. The letter includes a claim for damages, which follows an Oct. 23 ruling from the Second Appellate District. It held that a homeowner could seek damages when a city misses a mandatory permit deadline. That case involved an accessory dwelling unit, not AB 2011. Legal scholars have said its reasoning could reach other ministerial housing laws, including the one Rand cites. The state housing department has set a Nov. 25 deadline for Los Angeles to respond to its own letter. The department said it could refer the matter to the state attorney general. Where the threat has worked Other California cities have backed down when the cost of continuing to dig their heels in became clear. Glendale's council voted 4-1 last October to reject Trammell Crow Residential's 682-unit plan for a former Sears store. The project included 72 very low-income units. The state housing department issued a notice of violation Dec. 30. It warned of fines up to $34 million if the city did not reverse course. Glendale's council reversed its denial in late January, three months after rejecting the project. No lawsuit was filed, but the developer's attorney had called the case a "slam dunk" under the Housing Accountability Act. Morgan Hill in Silicon Valley took a similar path. City officials settled with High Street Residential , a builder's remedy developer, to avoid costly litigation with the developer and the state. The 105-home project had been hanging in legal limbo for three years. The city council unanimously approved it last week. Related More: Affordability Housing Policy

items.title: Real estate is moving toward more data privacy. Appraisers say UAD 3.6 is moving the other way
items.description: Monday marks the implementation date of UAD 3.6 , which requires appraisers to select specific data points from dropdown menus for every feature of a property, as opposed to writing text descriptions of the home as they previously did, increasing the amount of detail included in appraisal reports delivered to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac . Within UAD 3.6 is the new Certification 25, which has generated quite the buzz among appraisal professionals. Certification 25, which was established by the government sponsored entities (GSEs), expands the data reuse beyond the parameters set in UAD 2.6, which included Certification 21, which largely governed who could receive or distribute a physical appraisal report. Under Certification 25, entities that receive appraisal reports like lenders, GSEs, secondary market participants and data collection services to store, copy, reproduce, analyze, use and distribute all data within the report, including interior photos and property details, for internal or external purposes without needing the appraiser's further consent. While the certification does state that the appraiser and supervisory appraiser bear no liability for any use of the report outside of the specific mortgage finance transaction, appraisers are still concerned about this change and how it could impact their relationship with brokerages and real estate professionals. In posts on social media and articles written on Appraisers Blog, Desiree Mehbod, a Virginia-based appraiser, has raised concerns about what would happen if interior photos of a child’s bedroom with the property address are leaked, reproduced and shared, ultimately ending up on the dark web. “The biggest issue [with UAD 3.6] is Certification 25, which forces us to legally sign off that any downstream entity can permanently store, analyze, distribute and harvest our entire report data without our consent,” Mehbod told HousingWire . “Data privacy is incredibly important to people when it comes to their intimate spaces like bedrooms and bathrooms. When homeowners realize that the interior photos we take of their private living areas are being distributed to a long list of unknown third parties and permanent corporate tech archives, that trust is completely shattered.” Data privacy vs. data distribution For appraisers like Mehbod, it is noteworthy that these changes are coming at a time when privacy is becoming a hot topic among real estate professionals and consumers. From consumers asking their agents to remove listings photos from the internet after the sale of a home and the rise in private listings networks to MLS seeking to rein in who can use listing data and how , it seems that everyone wants increased data privacy and protection, but appraisers say Certification 25 is doing the opposite of that. “The listing side is building walls to protect consumer privacy, while the appraisal side is being forced to demand more data to feed a permanent corporate tech archive,” Mehbod said. “Reconciling this requires giving independent appraisers the exact same granular data controls and licensing protections that Realtors now have.” But the ability for downstream actors to have access to data like this is not new. According to Frank Gregoire, a Florida-based appraiser, Certification 25 is fairly similar to the statute it is replacing, Certification 21. “Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac maintain a proprietary database about every single dwelling that has ever had a loan on it,” Gregoire said. “So, the ability for downstream users to have access to that data has been there since these forms were introduced in the early 2000s. But, what is new is that it now specifies that the appraiser is aware that some parties may be using the data from their reports without their permission.” Who is getting this information? While Ryan Lundquist agrees that this is the only primary change with Certification 25, he still finds it incredibly concerning. “They can take the information and share it with whoever they want and the appraiser doesn’t have any control over that,” Lundquist, a Sacramento-based appraiser, said. "I know a lot of appraisers feel conflicted about that as it feels like it puts appraisers in a tough spot where a blank check to mine whatever data they want exists.” Lundquist said he would love to know who this information will be shared with or sold to. Gregoire is also concerned about appraisers including copyrighted data, such as images in the MLS in their report. “If the appraiser is an MLS participant, they are using that information under license and they are permitted to use it to support their valuation, but that is it, they cannot grant someone else the right to use that information and that is what's happening with Certification 25,” he said. Just the beginning for Certification 25? It is concerns like these that lead appraisers to say the discussion around Certification 25 is not over yet. “I don’t think it will sit well with a lot of people in real estate when they read or begin to understand how and where this data may be used,” Lundquist said. In addition, Mehbod said Certification 25 is why she and other like-minded appraisers have chosen to stop doing appraisal work for the GSEs. If a homebuyer wants their loan to close they have no choice but to allow the appraiser to generate a report, which Mehbod said will create “massive animosity right at the front door.” “It positions the appraiser as a forced data collector rather than an independent expert,” she said. “This friction damages public trust and opens a legal minefield for our profession, leaving appraisers highly vulnerable to consumer complaints and lawsuits from angry borrowers when transactions get messy over data harvesting policies they never wanted to participate in.” With UAD 3.6 just beginning to go into effect, it remains to be seen if anything regarding Certification 25 will change or how consumers and real estate brokers, agents and MLSs will respond. items.title: Rocket attacks broker conversion issues with new tool
items.description: Rocket attacks broker conversion issues with new tool By Colin McNamara Published November 03, 2026, 2:43 p.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Rocket Pro is launching a tool that will help mortgage brokers address conversion issues, as the lender continues its efforts to gain more wholesale business. Processing Content Part of Rocket's monthly Power Play initiative, the new app called Quick Counter allows brokers to build, adjust and deliver a competitive refinance loan estimate while the client is still on the phone, the company announced Tuesday. It will help loan officers avoid losing momentum due to callbacks. Austin Niemiec, Rocket chief revenue officer "The product itself is attacking the problem around conversion, especially in a really tough market ," Austin Niemiec, chief revenue officer at Rocket, told National Mortgage News. "Brokers can use Quick Counter to adjust the options and then deliver a real loan estimate that ensures they're competitive and they can win without stepping away from the conversation." The app builds on Rocket's investment in its wholesale channel and, similar to October's announcement, is a more permanent fixture in the lender's benefits for brokers. Last month, Rocket rolled out its Orbit platform, which provides brokers with advantages and perks that help them compete, ranging from more certainty on purchase loans to pricing flexibility when a deal needs help. Rocket also extended the pricing credit its broker partners can receive by working with a Compass buyer's agent . The partnership has generated $3 billion in rate locks since it was announced in February, the company said. "We are using our all-weather strength as a company to continue to invest and deliver value to brokers," Niemiec said. "These things are building off each other as a strategy where brokers take our technology and then take our fantastic pricing and use them to be more competitive and move faster when it comes to converting loans." The full launch included: The Quick Counter app built into Rocket Pro Navigate, the company's artificial intelligence hub for brokers; Live loan estimate generation for cash-out and rate-and-term refinances; Real-time adjustments to rates, points and loan terms; Options to evaluate lowest closing. Rocket doesn't yet have an estimate on the tool's expected effectiveness, but believes it will be one of the most used within Rocket Pro Navigate, Niemiec said. Quick Counter was West Capital Lending Broker Seth Hasan's winning idea from The Big Pitch competition at Rocket Pro's RPX event in September. "This was developed by a broker, voted by the entire broker community, and then we worked side by side with Seth and his team to make sure that we were bringing their vision to life," Niemiec said. items.description: Angel Oak posts 3Q GAAP loss as non-QM becomes challenging By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published November 03, 2026, 2:01 p.m. EST | Updated November 03, 2026, 7:46 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Processing Content Expert Quote: "During the quarter, non-QM and the fixed income market became more challenging" — Sreeni Prabhu, CEO and president Supporting Data: A $24 million hit to earnings from the company's securitization portfolio. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Distributable earnings for the third quarter Angel Oak Mortgage REIT were below estimates because of lower than expected net interest income, although the total economic return for the company's stock was better than BTIG's forecast, its post-earnings report said. On a GAAP basis, the non-qualified mortgage securitizer lost $16.7 million, compared with $3.4 million of net income in the second quarter and $11.4 million one year prior. The primary driver was a $24 million hit related to realized and unrealized net losses in its securitization portfolio, Brandon Filson, chief financial officer, said on the earnings call. How Angel Oak compared with other mREITs The BTIG report noted the consensus for distributable earnings was 4 cents per share over what Angel Oak reported. The REIT came in at 28 cents per share, and when realized gains on rate hedges are excluded, the miss to BTIG was 5 cents per share. "AOMR's economic book value performance is below the peer average of residential credit mREITs that have reported third-quarter book value so far, though we would note there is a wide range of 3Q book value performance (+2% to -20%)," wrote Douglas Harter, managing director at BTIG. Angel Oak's management said its business in the quarter was affected by macro factors in the market. Factors which impacted Angel Oak's results "During the quarter, non-QM and the fixed income market became more challenging as higher rates and a shift upward in the yield curve pressured asset valuation and compressed financing spreads across [the] mortgage credit market," said Sreeni Prabhu, CEO and president, on the earnings call. "While this environment negatively impacted book values across the landscape, as expected, Angel Oak's underlying credit performance of her portfolio remained stable and continued to perform in line with our expectations." Sreeni Prabhu, president and CEO at Angel Oak Mortgage REIT. Any valuation pressure reflects what is happening in the broader markets than any deterioration in credit quality or the underlying mortgage performance, which is an important distinction, Prabhu said. The REIT completed two securitizations in the quarter, before the height of the increase in interest rates. It has offered one so far in the current period, which Prabhu said was to mitigate further rate risk. Current market conditions are affecting Angel Oak's buying Lately, non-QM production has declined and the higher interest rate environment compressed returns on new investment. But Angel Oak is continuing to buy loans which meet its credit and return criteria. "We remain deliberate in pacing of our capital deployment across loan businesses and disciplined in maintaining underwriting standards that are central to our strategy, rather than extending risk and pursuing incremental returns at the expense of long-term credit performance," Prabhu said. However, a Bank of America Securities report from Oct. 30 noted the strong growth in non-QM originations which have come to market has not been reflected in the rate lock data. "We think this has to do with the increase in non-QM originators, with already more than 50 new originators in 2026," the report from Pratik Gupta, Chris Flanagan and Andy Fan said. "Either way, there is likelihood that rate lock is still underestimating the amount of supply that the non-QM market will see for this year and the beginning of 2027." Through Oct. 30, $100 million of non-QM issuance has been made during 2026 , up from $59 million at the start of July, B of A said. During the Q&A, Filson noted that typically these mortgages take 30-to-60 days to go through the lock process before they are closed and ready for securitization. Current returns are not quite as good as Angel Oak expects but they are starting to recover, he continued. But if the rate environment stays where it is, the set of locks the REIT gets through the next month will be back at return levels it expects. Management was asked about the state of the market, particularly if it is seeing more home equity line of credit business versus non-QM. From Angel Oak's perspective, the non-QM market remains strong, Filson said. In July, Angel Oak did a HELOC securitization with a current balance of $221.4 million. After the issuance, "we pulled back a little bit on the HELOC purchasing for the quarter, so we didn't really purchase too many in the quarter," Filson said. "But that's a switch and a valve that we could turn on and off very easily." Brad Finkelstein Originations Editor Brad Finkelstein is the originations editor of National Mortgage News. items.title: Newrez adds ex-Rocket exec, highlighting industry tech pivot
items.description: Newrez adds ex-Rocket exec, highlighting industry tech pivot By Spencer Lee CloseText About Spencer twitter Spencer_NYC linkedin spencer-lee-journo Published November 03, 2026, 1:39 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Expert Quote: "There is tremendous opportunity to build on that foundation and set a new standard in our industry for servicing excellence," — Newrez's Jay Jones. Forward Look: On the horizon: A scheduled transition to a new servicing platform starting in early 2027. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Processing Content Newrez added top servicing leader Jay Jones to its executive suite, marking another development in the mortgage industry's technology race, as recent appointments among the largest players demonstrate today's prioritization of artificial intelligence. Newrez Chief Servicing Officer Jay Jones The Fort Washington, Pennsylvania-based company named the former Rocket Mortgage leader chief servicing officer this week. Most recently, Jones held the same title at Rocket, the country's largest servicer. "Servicing is a foundation of our business, and bringing in someone of Jay's caliber speaks to the importance we place on our platform and servicing team," said Newrez President Baron Silverstein in a press release. Jones' appointment comes during a period of heightened consolidation within the home finance community , with leading mortgage researchers warning about the potential of a significant reduction in lending volume through 2027 . Although an ongoing wave of layoffs also looks likely to persist for several months, Newrez's move shows the pursuit of top-level tech-fluent executives continues among the largest companies despite industry downsizing. Jones previously served in senior management at Mr. Cooper, prior to its acquisition by Rocket in 2025, and played a pivotal role in integrating the servicing portfolios at the two mortgage giants. His career in mortgage servicing also includes tenures at Celink, OneWest Bank and IndyMac. Even while the outlook for originations gets bleaker, recent trends indicate some companies are willing to designate resources to build their servicing segments into business conduits , thanks to the recapture opportunities it offers. The mortgage industry's focus on tech and servicing strategy Upgraded servicing technology emerged as a primary focus of Newrez investment this year, even before a sudden surge in mortgage rates in second and third quarters destroyed prospects for a 2026 originations upturn. In February, its parent company, Rithm Capital, upped its investment into AI-backed servicing platform Valon Technologies, taking a minority ownership stake in the latter, while announcing plans to transfer its entire portfolio of loans onto the system. Company executives said during its recent earnings call that artificial intelligence investments across Newrez will drive $125 million in savings. Jones will lead transition efforts to the Valon platform beginning in early 2027, in addition to holding oversight of Newrez's $879 billion servicing portfolio. "Jay understands what our servicing clients and homeowners expect from us, and as we move to ValonOS, he will help build the next era of our industry-leading servicing experience," Silverstein said. In its most recent earnings, Rithm reported pre-tax income of almost $605 million at the mortgage unit. Servicing generated over $306 million in revenue to the bottom line. "Newrez has built a servicing business that clients trust and homeowners count on, pairing deep human expertise with strong digital capabilities. There is tremendous opportunity to build on that foundation and set a new standard in our industry for servicing excellence," Jones said. Tech expertise as a leadership prerequisite Newrez's announcement also shines a spotlight on the mortgage industry's propensity today to elevate technology experts to the highest positions, as companies look toward their futures when deciding to add or shuffle C-suite leadership. Prior to the blockbuster deal that joined Rocket and Mr. Cooper, Jones' former companies both were already making significant technology investments , even before the rapid growth of artificial intelligence. Two of the largest platforms used by lenders or servicers today, Dark Matter Technologies and Sagent, both opted to promote experienced software leaders Vikas Rao and Sridhar Sharma to CEOs of their respective companies in major leadership shakeups this year. Owners of the latter specifically cited the necessity of having technology expertise at the helm to lead it in the artificial intelligence age. items.title: Inspector general hits Pulte over 'unprecedented' obstruction
items.description: Inspector general hits Pulte over 'unprecedented' obstruction By Katy O'Donnell and Erin Schilling Published November 03, 2026, 10:52 a.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email The nation's top housing regulator took "unprecedented" steps to hinder investigations by its inspector general, the watchdog told lawmakers in a report published Monday. Processing Content The accusations – delivered in the Office of Inspector General's semiannual report to Congress – are the latest escalation in a feud between Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte and his congressionally mandated overseers. Pulte announced on social media in September that he would be slashing the OIG budget by more than 60%. The FHFA regulates Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the government-owned mortgage companies with $7.8 trillion in assets underpinning the mortgage market. Its inspector general is charged with policing mortgage fraud that could pose risk to their portfolios. It is also the office charged with investigating potential improprieties by agency leadership. Federal Housing Finance Agency Director William Pulte Eric Lee/Bloomberg "OIG's Office of Evaluations was unable to publish three reports" over the six months ending Sept. 30 "due to FHFA's refusal to provide enterprise records and information when requested," according to the report. Fannie and Freddie are sometimes called government-sponsored enterprises. But FHFA spokesman Jonathan Coppage said that the agency had "delivered every document and engaged in every interview the IG has requested under its statutory authorities." "FHFA has readily produced the hundreds of pages of documents and engaged in hours of interviews that the OIG requested regarding FHFA's oversight of Fannie and Freddie multifamily business," Coppage added. "For example, for just three recent reviews we completed 56 document requests and 16 separate hour-long meetings." In an unusual letter to lawmakers hours after Pulte announced the sweeping budget cuts on Sept. 30, Acting Principal Deputy Inspector General James Hodge said the office would be forced to cut up to 80% of its staff and end most criminal inquiries. That decision will have "devastating consequences," the new report concludes. "The unprecedented and abrupt cuts will prevent OIG from conducting meaningful oversight of FHFA going forward." Coppage pointed out that the inspector general had requested a budget much larger than those of other inspectors general. "Independence does not mean exemption from fiscal accountability," he said. "FHFA remains willing to work with OIG to offer what support it needs to effectively budget and exercise reasonable financial stewardship in carrying out its statutory responsibilities, as is customary in every federal agency." Hodge has maintained that the housing regulator watchdog is different from similar offices at other agencies because of the "enormous risks to the U.S. financial system inherent in the operations" of the entities FHFA regulates. Agency leadership has also "eviscerated" the inspector general's ability to investigate and deter mortgage and bank fraud, according to the report. OIG investigations over the past six months recovered $29 million and resulted in 46 indictments. Reuters earlier reported the OIG report, which was delivered to lawmakers Friday. items.title: Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac rally as Ackman presses for conservatorship exit
items.description: Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to Bill Ackman. Both stocks have moved more than 60% higher since Oct. 14. Ackman believes both names can see a "10-fold" increase from current share prices. Bill Ackman, chief executive officer of Pershing Square Capital Management LP, center, during the company's initial public offering (IPO) on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Wednesday, April 29, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to billionaire investor Bill Ackman. Investors may agree with him, if the rally in both stocks is any sign. The Federal National Mortgage Association, known as Fannie Mae, and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, or Freddie Mac, have each jumped more than 60% from Oct. 14 to Monday's close. The stocks were both up roughly 3% on Tuesday. Ackman, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, has long pushed for the two entities to be released from federal conservatorship. "The reason why it's not being touched right now is, you know, midterms," he said in an interview with CNBC's " Squawk Box ." Federal National Mortgage Association (Fannie Mae) and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation (Freddie Mac) over the last month. Ackman, who owns both names through Pershing Square, believes Freddie and Fannie have the potential to increase "10-fold from current share prices," he said in his quarterly letter to shareholders, issued on Monday. Fannie and Freddie buy mortgages from banks and other lenders, and then package them into mortgage-backed securities, known as MBS. Their operations are critical to the housing market, providing liquidity to banks and creating a secondary market for MBS. The entities were placed into conservatorship in September 2008, during the financial crisis. The stocks were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010 and have traded over the counter since then. Ackman wants the conservatorship to end, arguing the entities would be worth multiples of their current valuation if they were freed from government control. But it remains politically and economically contentious. The entities operate under strict capital threshold requirements and would need to be recapitalized, which could happen through issuing common equity. However, the Treasury Department would need to figure out an exit plan for its roughly $388 billion ownership stake in the entities through preferred securities and warrants. Congress may also need to play a role, passing legislation to restructure the government's role in mortgage financing and home-loan guarantees. Nonetheless, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently said it could happen before Trump's term ends, telling 2Way's " The Morning Meeting " podcast that the administration will tackle the ownership structure "next year, the year after." He said affordability will be guiding the decision. One point of controversy is whether ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie would increase the spreads on MBS over Treasuries, effectively making mortgages costlier. Bessent has sought to reassure the market that wouldn't happen. "Whatever we do is going to be guided by making sure that the spread on [agency] mortgages … over the Treasury does not increase," Bessent said. Ackman argues that privatizing the GSEs would help insulate them from political meddling. "Fannie and Freddie are these massive, enormously profitable institutions where whichever political party controls them…if they're still in conservatorship, can influence the outcome of elections," he told CNBC. In one scenario, he explained, Democrats win the White House, conservatorship is still in place, and Democrats push Fannie and Freddie to lower credit standards in order to expand home ownership and affordability. "If they're going to move more aggressively into borrowers with lower credit quality, for example, to achieve a political objective, that's going to have an impact on trillions of dollars outstanding mortgage securities," Ackman said. "It's going to have an impact on overall credit spreads." MBS investors want certainty about how the entities will be run, he noted. "That only gets resolved in a world in which they exit conservatorship, they become publicly traded companies that are owned by institutional and retail investors," Ackman said. "We set the rules. A key driver of this trend has been the Metro’s strong wage growth, with the median household income rising by 4.6% year-over-year (YOY) to $98,500. Phoenix’s population also grew at four times the rate of the national average, however, the 0.8% YOY increase marked a slowdown from previous quarters. Supply & Demand: Vacancy Plummets Amid Record Demand Net absorption across the Phoenix Metro reached 18,071 units year-to-date (YTD) through Q3 2026, already eclipsing the record annual total of 17,303 units set in 2024. All 15 multifamily submarkets recorded positive absorption for a third consecutive quarter, with Downtown (760 units), Deer Valley (752 units) and South West Valley (665 units) leading the overall market in Q3. Developers completed a six-year low of 2,008 units in Q3 2026. The slowdown in deliveries is likely to continue, with the active pipeline declining to 16,013 units, the lowest level since year-end 2019. During Q3, nine out of 15 submarkets observed no new openings, while just one—East Valley—accounted for 42% (835 units) of the Metro’s total. The East Valley is also the most active submarket for ongoing construction, with 3,838 units, or 24% of the market-wide pipeline. Pricing: Landlords Adjust Asking Rents To Aid Occupancy Rent trends from Q3 2026 suggested that landlords are generally continuing to temper marketed rates to unlock greater levels of renter demand, with the average level decreasing by 0.9% YOY to $1,590 per unit. This dynamic has been widespread, with 10 out of 15 multifamily submarkets posting YOY declines, ranging from 0.5% in the East Valley to 4.3% in Pinal County. Submarkets that observed YOY increases through Q3 include North Scottsdale (1.9%), Chandler (0.9%), Camelback (0.8%), Gilbert (0.4%) and Old Town Scottsdale (0.2%). Dr. Selma Hepp Cotality Chief Economist Insights from Chief Economist Dr. Selma Hepp As autumn arrived, the U.S. housing market cooled further. In September 2026, single-family home prices rose just 1.7% year-over-year and dropped 0.3% from August, pushing the national median above $400,000. This was the largest monthly decline since 2022 and the third consecutive September without growth, as high mortgage rates curbed summer demand. Normally, home prices edge up about 0.2% in September. But national averages still hide a key divide: Every Northeast and Midwest state saw annual price gains, while four Western and two Southern states posted declines. The market is nearly evenly split between areas accelerating and those slowing. Many Northeastern and Midwestern markets have gained 25% to 30% since mid-2022, while much of the West and Texas have seen little or no net growth. This regional divide sharpened considerably heading into the final stretch of the year. Chronic inventory shortages in the Great Lakes and New England fueled strong annual gains— Illinois (6.9%), Rhode Island (6.4%), Connecticut (6.0%), New Jersey (5.1%), and Ohio (4.9%). Meanwhile, prices dropped in former boom states: Washington (-1.0%), Wyoming (-0.7%), Texas (-0.4%), Hawaii (-0.1%), and Utah (-0.0%). Since June 2022, Rhode Island, Connecticut, and New Jersey have surged 30–31%, while Washington, Colorado, and Texas are up less than 1%, and D.C. is down 2%. “Potential homebuyers are feeling the pinch from rising costs across the board, especially for daily living expenses,” said Cotality Chief Economist Dr. Selma Hepp. “Meanwhile, limited job opportunities and slow wage growth are making households reluctant to move.” Leading metros for recent price growth include Cleveland, Albany, Providence, Greensboro, and St. Louis—places marked by affordability, job growth, in-migration, and recent price resets. In contrast, the fastest-cooling markets, like Augusta, Austin, Seattle, San Jose, and Washington, DC, have seen job losses, higher inventory, and declining affordability. Rising mortgage rates have sharply reduced affordability. When the 30-year fixed rate rose from 6.5% to 7.5%, the monthly payment on a median-priced home jumped $300, pushing the required annual income to $103,000. In California, buyers need $180,900 for a $754,500 median home. In Florida and Texas ($369,750 median), higher insurance and taxes often push total costs above borrowing limits, fueling declines in metros like Austin (-2.0%) and Dallas (-1.0%). “Elevated mortgage rates are expected to limit home buying opportunities in 2027,” concluded Dr. Hepp. “However, more inventory and greater buyer bargaining power will keep home price growth subdued, improving affordability.
